catalog_quote: p.67: From a general phonological point of view, the most interesting phenomenon is the development of a two-tone system where the tones are not the reflexes of voiced/voiceless proto-initials, as is most often the case in Mon-Khmer two-tone (or two-register) languages. Instead, the tones are the reflexes of the long/short vowel opposition which existed in Proto-Palaungic (inherited from Proto-Mon-Khmer). ... p.69: Minor syllables. As in other Northern Mon-Khmer languages, most non-compound words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic, i.e. consisting of a major syllable preceded by an unstressed minor syllable (cf. Shorto 1960). Minor syllables have a syllabic sonorant (such as m in θmphúp 'lung') or a (probably) non-contrasting vowel which I have written as a (kaʔà 'two'). ... p.71: Tones and vowels.
